extracted.intended_audience: military and government legal officers (judge advocates), War Department accounting and executive officers, and practitioners advising claimants against the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Digest of legal standards governing civilian employees (resignation, discharge, extra compensation, statutory prohibitions) and the substantive/administrative rules for presenting, reopening, and allowing claims against the United States. Focused on War Department practice and precedents (late 19th–early 20th century).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment for additional compensation for extra services
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an employee performs added duties that are separate and distinct from duties under his appointment, he may be paid for such extra services from the appropriation for that separate work; but where he performs added duties under his appointment at a single place, the statute provides that he shall receive no additional compensation for that class of duties unless special legislation so provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited (disbursing clerk of War Department performing clerical duties for Gettysburg National Park Commission could be legally paid from the Park appropriation). Authorities: C. 37Jf.7, Dec. 29, 1897; 10U6, May 22, 1901; 11026, Sept. 7, 1901; 12629, May 28, 1902; 21852, Aug. 16, 1907.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerks and messengers employment and salary controlled by Secretary of War (Aug. 6, 1894)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriation act approved August 6, 1894, provides that clerks and messengers 'shall be employed and apportioned to the several headquarters and stations by the Secretary of War.' They are to be employed by the Secretary at a particular specified salary, and department commanders have no power to discharge any of them or to increase or reduce their salaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional compensation for acting chief clerk requires Congressional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: An application by a clerk to be paid an amount in addition to his regular salary as compensation for services performed as acting chief clerk cannot be allowed except by authority of Congress (in view of provisions of sections 1764 and 1765, R. S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of resignation may be effective retroactively
rubrics_metrics.description: A resignation of an employee may be accepted to take effect upon the last day he worked even though that day is prior to the date the resignation was accepted; acceptance merely amounts to a declaration of the fact that the employee separated himself from the service on the prior date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to resign where tenure unspecified; abandonment not ground to withhold pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a civilian accepted Government employment as a clerk with no understanding as to tenure of office, the clerk had the right to resign when he saw fit, and his abandonment of the service (on a refusal to forward his resignation for acceptance) is no legal ground for withholding his pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation acceptance becomes irrevocable after due notice communicated
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule governing acceptance of a clerk's resignation is similar to that for officers: after due notice of the acceptance has been communicated, there can be no withdrawal of the tender or revocation of the acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation tender should be rejected if employee under civil-service investigation; dismissal required
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a civil-service employee who had displayed political activity and was under investigation for violating civil-service rules tendered his resignation to take effect immediately, the resignation should not be accepted; rather, the employee should be dismissed for violation of the civil-service rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality and irrevocability of discharges
rubrics_metrics.description: A legally executed discharge is beyond recall; the ultimate discharge of a civil employee as of the date of his suspension is lawful; a discharge that has been executed cannot be revoked and to substitute permission to resign for the discharge would falsify the record; mere mistake by officers in recommending or issuing the discharge will not justify its revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation for work-related injuries governed by statute of May 30, 1908
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to May 30, 1908, no payments could lawfully be made to civil employees for damages for personal injuries or for medical/surgical expenses out of the appropriation for the work unless medical/surgical treatment was provided for in the contract of employment. For cases arising after May 30, 1908, relief should be measured by the requirements of the act of May 30, 1908 (35 Stat. 556) as amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority and guidance: C. 23069, Apr. 14, 1908; note references to later amendments (Feb. 24, 1909; Mar. 4, 1911) and the restricted classes covered by the act (artisans, laborers in specific government establishments, hazardous employment on specified projects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute's compensation includes subsistence and may be commuted
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision of the act of May 30, 1908 that an employee's compensation shall be 'the same pay as if he continued to be employed' is construed as including subsistence in cases where subsistence was furnished at the time of the accident; payment of compensation may take the form of commutation of rations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation based on a Secretary of Commerce and Labor letter dated June 30, 1910; authority: C. 23069, July 18, 1910.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory scope limits coverage for injury relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief under the May 30, 1908 act is limited to the classes and activities enumerated by the statute; persons injured while performing work not within the statute's scope (e.g., a carpenter injured while working on a bridge acquired for West Point water supply) are not covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilian employees temporarily armed or serving in defense remain civilians for civil-service status
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerks employed as an armed force to protect public property and to assist in defense were held not to be in the military service proper but to remain civilians; service until no longer required did not place them in the status of being 'honorably discharged' for civil-service appointment purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Service in war' in uniform regulations applies to military personnel only
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'service in war' as used in uniform regulations relates to service as an officer or enlisted man in the military establishment and does not attach to the status of a civil employee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilian abandonment of employment is not desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil employee of the Quartermaster's Department does not become liable as a deserter by abandoning his employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seaman discharge and wage entitlement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A seaman discharged voluntarily at a foreign port is entitled to wages up to the time of discharge but not beyond; unless the time has expired or the voyage for which the seaman shipped has been completed, he should not be discharged in a foreign port where he is liable to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive order prohibiting usurious loans by employees
rubrics_metrics.description: An executive order of April 13, 1911 prohibits clerks or other civilian employees in or under the War Department (or military establishment) from loaning money at usurious rates either as principal or agent, directly or indirectly; an employee serving as treasurer of a society making such loans falls within the language 'principal or agent' and is within the prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception permits appointment of additional drivers without examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory exception from civil-service examination requirements regarding one driver of carriage for the head of an executive department, followed by the words 'and such other drivers of carriages as may from time to time be authorized by competent authority,' permits appointment, without examination, of a second driver for the Secretary of War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of vouchers when an authorized official dies (section 173 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a commissioner appointed under a statute dies leaving uncertified vouchers for salary due a clerk of the commissioner, under section 173 R. S. the chief clerk of the War Department should certify the vouchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head of department generally has no authority to reopen a claim once duly settled
rubrics_metrics.description: Under executive practice, a head of a department is generally not empowered, without specific statutory authority, to reopen a claim or controversy once duly settled by his predecessor; a successor may reopen only for fraud, lack of jurisdiction, manifest error on the face of the proceedings, or newly discovered evidence presented within a reasonable time and sufficient to warrant a new trial in law. Any public officer may, however, correct his own errors and reopen cases decided by himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities and elaboration: Rollins and Presbrey v. U. S. and departmental practice; numerous Comptroller and Attorney General opinions cited (e.g., P. 34, 225, Aug. 1, 1889; 9 Op. Atty. Gen. 34). Reopening based on resolutions or committee reports is permissible for reexamination but such committee views are not binding; the Secretary must follow the statute and his own judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final statutory settlement estops claimant from reopening claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A final settlement of a claim under special statutory authority followed by receipt and acceptance by the claimant of the amount awarded estops the claimant from questioning that such allowance and payment constituted a full and final satisfaction of his entire claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Secretary of War's settlement of a railroad company's claim for military transportation paid and accepted as final; without new authority from Congress the Secretary could not reopen the case except to correct errors in calculation. Authority: R. 42, 332, June 17, 1879.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule: executive/accounting officers cannot allow unliquidated damages absent Congressional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, neither the Secretary of War nor any executive or accounting officer, in the absence of authority from Congress, is empowered to entertain, allow, settle, or pay a claim for unliquidated damages (damages in the legal sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: claims for indemnity for wrongful arrests, damages to property by troops, etc. Authorities and cases cited: B. 42, 592, Apr. 13, 1880; Dennis v. U. S. and others. The rule does not forbid payments for work or materials actually furnished and received under a contract, though the price is not fixed by the contract; such contractual claims arise from executed agreements and are within accounting processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between contractual unliquidated claims and damages founded on neglect or breach
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for money due on contracts where exact amount is not fixed are technically 'unliquidated damages' but arise from executed agreements and are normally susceptible to accounting; by contrast, claims for unliquidated damages founded on neglect or breach of obligations (not necessarily arising from contract) require extraneous proof and judicial liquidation and are not committed to Treasury accounting officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted summary from Dennis v. U. S.: contractual claims are determinable by vouchers/reports; breach-based claims involve broad investigation and are for the courts (see Power's case, Brannen's case, Cramp & Sons v. U. S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may use supplemental contracts to settle certain claims but cannot settle breach-based unliquidated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding the general rule, where it is not against the interest of the United States, the Secretary of War may enter a supplemental contract with a contractor discontinuing or modifying an existing contract and settling all claims arising thereunder; however, no executive or accounting officer has authority to settle by supplemental contract unliquidated claims arising from a breach of the contract — such claims must be liquidated by courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: U. S. v. Corliss Engine Co., Satterlee v. U. S., Cramp & Sons v. U. S., and Comptroller/Attorney General opinions cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriations or statutory language may make exceptions for payment of unliquidated damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule against payment of unliquidated damages is subject to statutory exceptions — e.g., where an appropriation authorizes 'leases of land and damages of property' or where the law implies a contract to pay rent/damages, unliquidated damages may be payable under that statutory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: where an act of Congress appropriated money for 'leases of land and damages of property' it would include unliquidated damages (C. 16525, May 19, 1904); see also annotations regarding Organized Militia expenditures.
